symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown with a rough, slightly raised look, often with a yellow halo. Badly hit leaves drop, and scabby raised spots can appear on fruit.
organic_treatment: Remove and bag badly spotted leaves; water at the base, not overhead; avoid touching wet plants; clean tools between plants; use certified clean seed and rotate away from pepper and tomato. Copper-based sprays used in organic systems give only partial protection.
chemical_treatment: There is no cure. Copper-based bactericides (often mixed with mancozeb where registered) can slow spread if started early, before spots are widespread. Use only products registered for pepper in your area, follow the label for the waiting period and safety gear, and combine with the clean-practice steps.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms: leaves are an even green with no spots, curling, mottling or webbing.
organic_treatment: Routine care: water at the base, space plants for airflow, mulch, rotate crops and inspect leaves weekly.
chemical_treatment: None needed. Do not spray healthy plants as a precaution without local advice.

symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (a target look) on older, lower leaves first, often with a yellow halo. Spots merge, leaves dry up and drop, and stems and tubers can also be marked.
organic_treatment: Remove heavily infected lower leaves; avoid overhead watering late in the day; rotate crops; destroy plant debris after harvest; keep plants well fed and watered because stressed plants are hit harder. Copper-based or Bacillus-based biological sprays are used in organic systems with partial effect.
chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb (where registered) applied at the first symptoms or in blight-prone weather; stronger systemic types such as strobilurins or triazoles are used under heavy pressure. Rotate between groups to slow resistance, follow the label and waiting period, and check local registration.

symptoms: Pale green to brown water-soaked patches on leaves, often with white fuzzy growth underneath in damp weather, dark streaks on stems, and fast collapse of the plant. Tubers can show reddish-brown dry rot under the skin.
organic_treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost); use healthy seed tubers; hill soil over tubers; improve airflow; avoid wet foliage; destroy volunteer potatoes; do not store suspect tubers with healthy ones. Copper-based sprays in organic systems protect only if applied before infection.
chemical_treatment: Act early: preventive protectant fungicides (such as mancozeb, chlorothalonil or copper-based products, where registered) before infection; under heavy pressure local services may advise systemic or translaminar products such as cymoxanil or dimethomorph mixtures. Sprays do not cure infected tissue. Follow the label, waiting period and local blight alerts, and rotate groups.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms: leaves are an even green with no spots, wilting or yellowing.
organic_treatment: Routine care: use healthy seed tubers, water at the base, hill soil over tubers, rotate crops and inspect leaves weekly.
chemical_treatment: None needed. Do not spray healthy plants as a precaution without local advice.

symptoms: Small dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo; the centres can drop out and leave ragged leaves. Raised, rough scabby spots appear on green fruit.
organic_treatment: Remove and bag badly spotted leaves; avoid handling wet plants; use drip or base watering; clean tools; use certified clean seed and transplants and rotate away from tomato and pepper for 2-3 years. Copper-based sprays used in organic systems give only partial protection.
chemical_treatment: There is no cure. Copper-based bactericides (often mixed with mancozeb where registered) can slow spread if started early, before spots are widespread. Use only products registered for tomato in your area, follow the label for the waiting period and safety gear, and combine with the clean-practice steps.

symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings on older leaves, often with a yellow halo; dark sunken areas can appear on stems and near the fruit stalk. Lower leaves yellow and fall first.
organic_treatment: Remove infected lower leaves; mulch to stop soil splash; stake plants for airflow; water at the base; rotate crops; clear debris after harvest; choose tolerant varieties. Copper-based or Bacillus-based biological sprays have a partial effect.
chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper-based products (where registered) from the first symptoms; strobilurin-type systemic products may be used under heavy pressure. Rotate groups to slow resistance, follow the label and waiting period, and check local registration.

symptoms: Large greasy grey-green to brown blotches on leaves, dark patches on stems and firm brown blotches on fruit, with white fuzzy growth underneath in humid weather. It spreads very fast in cool, wet conditions.
organic_treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost); isolate from healthy plants and nearby potatoes; use healthy transplants; improve airflow; avoid wet foliage. Copper-based sprays in organic systems protect only if applied before infection.
chemical_treatment: Act early: preventive protectant fungicides (such as mancozeb, chlorothalonil or copper-based products, where registered) before infection; under heavy pressure local services may advise systemic or translaminar products such as cymoxanil or dimethomorph mixtures. Sprays do not cure infected tissue. Follow the label, waiting period and local blight alerts, and rotate groups.

symptoms: Pale green or yellow patches on the upper side of older leaves with a velvety olive-green to brown mold on the matching underside. Leaves curl, wither and drop, mostly in humid, poorly ventilated conditions.
organic_treatment: Improve ventilation (open vents, prune, widen spacing); lower humidity; avoid wetting leaves and water in the morning; remove affected leaves; choose resistant varieties; clean greenhouse structures between crops.
chemical_treatment: If better ventilation alone does not stop it, protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil or copper-based products (where registered) may be used. Resistance can develop quickly, so rotate groups, follow the label and waiting period, and check local registration.

symptoms: Many small round spots with grey-white centres and dark edges, often with tiny black dots in the middle. It starts on lower leaves, which yellow and drop, leaving fruit exposed to sun.
organic_treatment: Remove infected lower leaves; mulch to stop soil splash; keep leaves dry and water at the base; rotate crops for 2 years; stake plants; clear debris after harvest. Copper-based or Bacillus-based biological sprays have a partial effect.
chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper-based products (where registered) from the first spots, repeated while wet weather lasts. Rotate groups, follow the label and waiting period, and check local registration.

symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckles on leaves that merge into a bronzed, dusty look; fine webbing on the underside and between leaves in bad cases. Leaves dry out and fall, especially in hot, dry weather.
organic_treatment: Spray plants with a firm jet of water, especially the underside of leaves; reduce dust and raise humidity; remove badly infested leaves; use insecticidal soap, neem or horticultural oil with thorough coverage; protect or release predatory mites.
chemical_treatment: Use a miticide only when mites are confirmed and spreading (for example abamectin, spiromesifen or sulfur-based products, where registered for tomato). Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides such as pyrethroids, which often make mite outbreaks worse by killing natural enemies. Rotate groups, follow the label and waiting period, and ask local extension for approved products.

symptoms: Brown spots with ring patterns and a pale centre (like a target) on leaves, plus dark sunken spots on fruit. Spots can merge, causing yellowing and leaf drop.
organic_treatment: Remove infected leaves; prune and space plants for airflow; keep leaves dry and water at the base; rotate crops; clear plant debris after harvest; avoid dense planting.
chemical_treatment: Protectant fungicides such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb or copper-based products (where registered); strobilurin-type systemic products may be used under heavy pressure. Rotate groups to slow resistance, follow the label and waiting period, and check local registration.

symptoms: Leaves curl upward and become small, thick and yellow at the edges; plants are stunted and bushy, flowers drop and few fruit set, especially if infection happens early.
organic_treatment: There is no cure. Remove and destroy infected plants early (bag them); control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps, reflective mulch, insect-proof netting over nurseries and weed removal; use resistant or tolerant varieties and inspect transplants. Neem or soap sprays may reduce whitefly numbers but do not cure the virus.
chemical_treatment: No chemical cures a virus. Chemicals only target the whitefly that spreads it: rotating groups of insecticides (for example insect growth regulators, spiromesifen or systemic neonicotinoids, where registered) can reduce spread, mainly in nurseries and early growth. Follow the label and waiting period, protect pollinators, and ask local extension for approved products.

symptoms: Light and dark green mottling (mosaic) on leaves, sometimes with narrow, twisted or fern-like leaves; stunted growth; fruit may ripen unevenly with brown patches inside.
organic_treatment: There is no cure. Remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost); wash hands with soap and disinfect tools with a household bleach solution or trisodium phosphate, then rinse; do not handle healthy plants after infected ones; avoid tobacco before touching plants; use clean seed and resistant varieties and control weeds.
chemical_treatment: No chemical treatment cures this virus, and fungicides and insecticides do not help. Control is by hygiene: disinfect hands and tools (follow the disinfectant label), use clean seed and resistant varieties, and remove infected plants early.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms: leaves are an even green with no spots, curling, mottling or webbing.
organic_treatment: Routine care: water at the base, stake and space plants for airflow, rotate crops and inspect leaves weekly.
chemical_treatment: None needed. Do not spray healthy plants as a precaution without local advice.
